title: Better Differences Between Physical and Magic?

posts.author: LordOfPotatos
posts.body:
What's a good way to make physical and magic offense different from the other?
some approaches I've seen are using different resources (like HP/SP in SMT), physical attacks having access to crits or weapon effects or magic attacks having perfect accuracy.
but these are all pretty standard, so what else is there? any ideas?

posts.author: EF2L
posts.body:
What I did is making physical attack can be used multiple times immediately in one turn (like Chrono Cross) with limited total cost per turn to spend. So, each weapon will have its own set of skills with varying accuracy depending on effect and damage. For example:
Sword: 5 Action Points (AP).
Quick (cost 1 AP): 50% damage| 60% hit rate,
Normal (cost 2 AP): 85% damage| 85% hit rate,
Heavy (cost 3 AP): 150% damage, defense pierce 30%| 70% hit rate
Focus (cost 1 AP): Hit rate +15% for next attack (stackable.)
Then you can either gamble for bigger damage or select whichever moves suits the situation the best. Of course, there is also supplemental equipment/states that will help with accuracy, enhance specific weapon skill(s), boost AP, and many others.
You could also implement durability and make weapon that can be carried/found limited to make player not stick to one type of gameplay and experiment more with what they have, I guess. (Though I don't think this is applicable if you have many characters and can just swap to other party member for different gameplay.)
For Magic I make it powerful and sure hit but also comes with limitation. Magic will cost MP to use but if your MP hits 0 any negative states have 100% chance to apply on you. Skills that apply negative ailments like Sleep, Confusion, etc. instead damage your MP at first without applying it, if your MP is/reduced to 0 you will be unable to recover MP for 1.5 turn and in that state you're vulnerable to many negative states. If you keep it from going to 0 instead it will have natural % MP regen at the start of your turn that helps you maintain it above 0.
So, it becomes a trade-off mechanic where you either used it as a shield against powerful detrimental ailments like Sleep that skip your turn(s) and double the first damage you take or go full offensive with big damage until you ran out of juice.
You can also go wacky and add more effect to your magic like, use more MP to immediately use skill without skipping your turn, change single target to all, added bonus effect and many more.
In the end I'm still experimenting, there should be a better implementation to differ Physical and Magic from the others.

Click to expand...
The way I handle it is by literally splitting them apart. They count as separate things both in the UI (eg. you see the symbols in your skill menu and when the enemy skill text pops up in combat), which stats use them and have several states dedicated to the difference.
Physical ▲
is orange, and always uses your Strength stat unless stated otherwise. It's reduced by
Defense
.
Magical ★
is blue, and always uses your Spirit stat unless stated otherwise. It's reduced by
Resistance
.
Physical attacks are bounced back by Power Shield, while Magical attacks are bounced back by Reflect. You can't have both shields on at the same time, so in some situations having a healthy mix of attacks can be better than having someone who ultra-specializes in one type of attack.
Thorn Crest
is a passive ability that hurts the attacker for 33% of the damage you dealt if you made contact, and a lot of Physical moves tend to be contact-based unless you're throwing something. So magic would be a good way to avoid this.
Like I'm a person that likes to keep it simple:
Sometimes just having a mecha-saurus that has 999 physical defense but 5 magical defense is enough.
I always wince a bit whenever I see an RPG where a character's physical and magical attacks are pretty much the same in power, but one type has elements or uses an MP gauge or something.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm... not sure what the question is asking.  Or... why it's being asked, I guess?
I mean, you have the usual difference:
Physical attacks use weapons and the Attack stat to deal damage.
Magical attacks use skills, the Magic stat to deal damage, and consume MP or Spell Slots to activate.  They're also more powerful than physical attacks, generally.
Then, there's other differences:
Magic attacks have access to elemental damage like Fire, Water, Lightning, Ice, etcetera.
Physical attacks have access to physical damage like Blunt, Piercing, Slashing.
Magic attacks have access to magical states.  Burn, Silence, Slow, Stop, etcetera.
Physical attacks have access to physical states.  Stun, Poison, etcetera.
Magic attacks are reflected by Reflect.
Physical attacks are reflected by Counter.
Magic attacks generally AOE (multi-target).
Physical attacks generally single target.
Magic attacks are strong against physically defensive enemies.
Physical attacks are strong against magically defensive enemies.
I'm not quite sure what you're asking for.  I think any "difference" between them is something that was "already used" before in another game.  Or is just another flavor of one of the above generalizations.
I mean, the most "different" I make them in my own game is just that mages can also have an "Attack" like command that uses Magic to damage without consuming MP, and their "Magic" stat.  Well, that, and maybe how the equipment for the Witch works (with spellbooks as shields, granting immunity to specific elements, and wands as weapons causing "weakness to X element" 100% of the time on hit.
But, it all just boils down to one thing in any RPG:
Physical and Magical are just categories for defining the damage type, so that combat has a little more strategy or depth than it would otherwise.  What's the difference between a Sword Strike that does 60 damage, and a Fire Spell that does 60 damage, if the enemy is neutral to all elements involved in those?
Nothing.  No difference.  Other than visual and "flavor text".

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body:
One option is to essentially remove the cooked in differences and create your own categories like:
Melee
- (close, usually physical)
Range
- (far, usually physical)
Magic
- (any range, almost always magic, single target or small area)
Area
- (magic or physical) large AoE.
Damage formula determines what stats affect damage and defense per skill.  If you turn your main types into elements, you can affect offense and defense by category.  Modify the default "physical" and "magical" to have little effect except to determine how counterattacking/reflection will be handled for the skill.
There are many twists that can be used as noted by others.  Another example:
MP - As MP becomes depleted, OFF/DEF/MAT/MDF  increases or decreases slightly/moderately.
AP - As AP becomes depleted, OFF/DEF/MAT/MDF increases or decreases slightly/moderately.
This can add an extra tactical layer to combat, and give distinction to MP use vs AP use.

In my game, all skills use mp.
Physical skills can miss.
(Magical skills can be ineffective due to elemental resistance, but can never miss.)

I'm not sure if your asking the right question. There are many ways to distinguish physical and magical offensive abilities from each other but the key, at least in my opinion, is to have the differences set out through your story/narrative and to remain consistent with it.
In the game I'm working on, physical runs off TP while magic runs on MP. However, because magic is not inherent to humans, they won't have an mp bar. Only through equiping a piece of equipment, you'll gain access to the magic menu and actually get mp to use spells.
I may add additional things as I get further in development but the key is to have a concept of the framework and that may require you looking at the world that your story is set in.

Click to expand...
This is one of those things developers think they need to overcomplicate, but most players don't care.
My approach is nearly always this, and nothing more/less:
[Physical]
- Typed as "physical" so physical hit, accuracy, physical mitigation, etc apply
- Usually (but not always) it's the attacker's atk stat checked against the target's def stat
- Most (but not all) take on the weapon's attributes (damage types, states if any, etc)
[Magical]
- Typed as "magical" so magic evasion, reflect, magical mitigation, etc apply
- Usually (but not always) it's the attacker's mat stat checked against the target's mdf stat
- Fixed damage type(s) in most cases
So again, not complicated.
A warrior would have mostly physical attacks and be good against enemies with low physical mitigation/def/evasion/etc.  They'd be able to influence most of their attack skills' damage types by equipping different weapon, or may even have some fixed damage type abilities.
A wizard would have a variety of damage types for flexibility regardless of weaponry, with them almost all being fixed damage types.  They'd be best against enemies resistant to physical damage, but less so to magical damage.  They'd need to worry about things like reflect though, which the warrior doesn't need care about at all.

posts.author: LotusOmaha8
posts.body:
It usually helps to keep it fairly simple (not over-complicated at least) on the hero side, just the tried-and-true differences are mostly enough...except perhaps any that are introduced through your specific worldbuilding.
Meanwhile on the enemy side is where much of the effort and creativity should be made. As in how they react to or are affected by each attack, or combinations of attacks. Without knowing your specific worldbuilding, it's hard to give specific examples - but put yourself in the player's shoes and it should feel intuitive, fun, challenging, and interesting / not monotonous.
Part of the reasoning here is that over the course of the game, enemies tend to change much more than the heroes. And they are mainly what the player is focused on, especially as the enemy dictates the challenge. So having a broad range of potential challenges is usually not a bad idea.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
One of the general differences for them in my game is that the vast majority of skills are single target and AoEs are far more common amongst the spells. Outside of skills tied to specific weapons or weapon types, a character that uses skills primarily focus targets one at a time while a character that uses spells primarily will generally have AoEs available.
AoE skills also tend to do less damage to each successive target as they dampen with each hit. It's the case for every AoE "swing" skill that the primary target takes full damage, but the 2nd target may only take 90%, the 3rd 80% and so on.
Spells are entirely exempt, but a few of the more powerful ones specifically do less damage based on the number of active targets.
I say skill and spell because at some point I ended up splitting hit type from damage type and needed the distinction. I didn't feel like how it already worked meshed with how I wanted them to work. Most skills do physical damage and most spells do magical damage, but there are plenty of each that use another damage type.
Most earth spells in my game deal physical damage since they're mostly creating/manipulating physical objects to deal damage. They're still magic, can be silenced, and trigger spell effects, but they also use the target's physical resistance and trigger physical hit effects instead of magic.
Meanwhile stuff like MCH's flamethrower is the opposite. It's a fire skill with magical damage and uses the target's magical resistance, but cannot be reflected as it's not a spell, is affected by HIT/EVA, and burns caused by it use the user's ATK at the time of the skill being used instead of the user's current MAT at the end of each turn.
